consumer_seed: The Ofcom mobile-reception guide was published on 27 May 2022.
Ofcom's coverage checker can show indoor and outdoor coverage for telephone, 3G and 4G services and outdoor availability of 5G.
The coverage checker can be used in an internet browser with a postcode or device location.
The checker provides an at-a-glance summary and an interactive map for the selected area.
Coverage-checker information is supplied by mobile operators and updated regularly.
Coverage predictions are generated by computer models that simulate how mobile signals travel.
Ofcom warns that prediction models may not always represent actual coverage on the ground.
Ofcom undertakes measurements to assess the accuracy of operator-supplied coverage data.
Coverage checkers indicate likely coverage at a fixed location rather than guaranteeing it.
Ofcom advises checking coverage at frequently visited places such as work and commuting locations.
Walls, metal frames, ceilings, pillars and basement rooms can impair indoor mobile coverage.
Hills and large buildings can block mobile signals.
Mobile signals can be degraded inside a vehicle.
A phone's design and antennas affect its ability to receive mobile signals.
For telephone and text use in poor-coverage areas, some basic handsets can receive better than smartphones.
Wi-Fi calling may help where mobile coverage is poor but Wi-Fi is good, subject to network and handset compatibility.
Consumer contract rules may allow cancellation without charge within 14 calendar days of signing up.
A monthly SIM-only or pay-as-you-go service can be used to test another provider without a long-term contract.
Connecting a phone to Wi-Fi can provide data service and avoid using the mobile contract's data allowance.
A mobile repeater uses an outdoor mobile signal to improve indoor coverage and works best with a strong outdoor signal.
The Ofcom mobile-switching page was published on 3 April 2023.
Keeping a mobile number when changing provider is called porting.
A customer who wants to keep a number requests a Porting Authorisation Code and gives it to the new provider.
Auto-Switch can be used for one number or multiple numbers up to 24.
For one number, a PAC can be requested by texting PAC to 65075.
A PAC requested by phone must be provided immediately or by text within two hours if immediate provision is not possible.
A PAC requested by text or online must be provided within two working days.
For two to 24 numbers, a PAC can be requested online or by phone.
A switch involving more than 24 numbers requires direct instructions from the current provider.
A PAC is valid for 30 days and a new one can be requested after expiry.
The current provider must send information such as early termination charges alongside the PAC.
After the new provider receives the PAC, the number should normally be ported within one working day.
A customer who does not want to keep the number requests a Service Termination Authorisation Code.
For one number, a STAC can be requested by texting STAC to 75075.
Mobile providers may not charge for notice periods that run after the switch date.
The Ofcom unwanted-calls, texts and emails guide was published on 15 July 2026.
Ofcom distinguishes nuisance marketing, spam and unsolicited contact from scams.
A live marketing caller must identify the company and provide a contact number.
A live marketing caller must stop if the recipient asks the company to stop calling.
A company should not make live marketing calls to a Telephone Preference Service registrant without specific consent.
Automated marketing calls require explicit consent.
For a known marketing-text sender or shortcode, replying STOP can opt out without a charge.
Ofcom advises not replying to an unknown marketing-text sender because a reply confirms the number is active.
An unwanted text can be forwarded free to 7726 for reporting to the phone company.
For a legitimate recognised company, the unsubscribe link can be used for unwanted marketing email.
For an unknown or suspicious email, Ofcom advises not clicking links and marking it as spam or junk.
A silent call is a call where the recipient hears nothing and cannot tell whether anyone is on the line.
Ofcom published the new mobile-messaging scam protections on 15 July 2026.
Mobile providers must collect information about scam messages, malicious links and phone numbers from customers and anti-fraud organisations.
Mobile providers must block numbers used by scammers and prevent messages being sent from them.
Mobile providers must identify and block scam messages in transit using malicious links and phone numbers.
Mobile providers must set volume limits for pay-as-you-go SIM cards.
Using a separate Bluetooth earpiece can improve reception compared with holding the phone next to the ear.
Calling apps can make and receive calls over Wi-Fi but do not typically use the mobile phone number.
Some operator home devices connect to a router and carry traffic over broadband to improve mobile signal.
Some train operators provide Wi-Fi and may include Wi-Fi-calling options.
Using a handheld mobile device while driving is illegal unless hands-free access is used.
A phone in a dashboard cradle may receive better in-vehicle coverage than one in a central console or footwell.
Ofcom states that an external vehicle aerial could provide good in-vehicle coverage on up to 20% more of the UK road network.
A global roaming SIM may be an option for frequent overseas travel, subject to provider prices.
A dual-SIM solution can help where different providers cover different locations.
PAC or STAC information allows the old and new providers to avoid double payment during a switch.
A switch taking more than one working day or involving process abuse can create a right to reasonable compensation.
A customer can ask the new provider to port a cancelled number for free within one month of cancellation.
Persistent nuisance marketing calls, texts or emails can be reported to the Information Commissioner's Office.
Companies using diallers must display a number, and landline users can try 1471 after a silent or abandoned call.
Ofcom advises recording the number, time and frequency of silent or abandoned calls.
A phone company can advise when the caller behind silent or abandoned calls cannot be identified.
Persistent silent or abandoned calls can be reported to Ofcom with caller and frequency details.
Ofcom may investigate repeated abandoned or silent calls and can impose fines of up to £2 million.
expansion_rule: Join verified monthly contract seeds by normalized contract name. Retain exactly the 35 contracts with all ten monthly built values. Emit eighteen time-series records per contract: observed-month count, minimum, maximum, range, mean, median, population standard deviation, minimum month, maximum month, increase count, decrease count, unchanged count, longest non-decreasing run, direction-change count, total absolute movement, first-to-last net movement, coefficient of variation, and a volatility classification. Append 70 Ofcom records. Every fifth record is REVALIDATION; all others are UPGRADE.
